questions.stem: This stellate cell bearing numerous spiny membrane processes specializes in capturing antigen and priming naive T cells. What is it?

explanation.summary: The characteristic star-shaped morphology with many long processes marks a dendritic cell, the most effective professional antigen-presenting cell for activating naive T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The characteristic star-shaped morphology with many long processes marks a dendritic cell, the most effective professional antigen-presenting cell for activating naive T cells.

questions.stem: The diagram follows a dendritic cell capturing antigen in skin and presenting it to a naive T cell in the lymph node. Besides peptide-MHC recognition, what second signal must the dendritic cell deliver to fully activate the naive T cell?

explanation.summary: Naive T-cell activation requires signal 1 (peptide-MHC engaging the TCR) plus signal 2, costimulation through B7 (CD80/86) on the mature dendritic cell binding CD28 on the T cell. CCR7 guides the DC to the T-cell zone; without costimulation the T cell becomes anergic.
explanation.whyCorrect: Naive T-cell activation requires signal 1 (peptide-MHC engaging the TCR) plus signal 2, costimulation through B7 (CD80/86) on the mature dendritic cell binding CD28 on the T cell. CCR7 guides the DC to the T-cell zone; without costimulation the T cell becomes anergic.

questions.stem: The figure contrasts antigen capture in lymph nodes (tissue antigens) with capture in the organ that filters blood-borne antigens. Loss of that blood-filtering organ leaves patients especially vulnerable to which pathogens?

explanation.summary: The spleen captures and clears blood-borne antigens and opsonized encapsulated organisms via its marginal zone. Asplenic or hyposplenic patients are at high risk of overwhelming infection by encapsulated bacteria and require vaccination and prophylaxis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The spleen captures and clears blood-borne antigens and opsonized encapsulated organisms via its marginal zone. Asplenic or hyposplenic patients are at high risk of overwhelming infection by encapsulated bacteria and require vaccination and prophylaxis.

questions.stem: The oxidative (respiratory) burst diagrammed here is defective in a phagocyte immunodeficiency causing recurrent catalase-positive infections. Which test confirms that diagnosis?

explanation.summary: A defect in the NADPH oxidase that generates superoxide causes chronic granulomatous disease. The DHR and NBT tests measure the phagocyte oxidative burst; failure to oxidize the dye confirms CGD.
explanation.whyCorrect: A defect in the NADPH oxidase that generates superoxide causes chronic granulomatous disease. The DHR and NBT tests measure the phagocyte oxidative burst; failure to oxidize the dye confirms CGD.

questions.stem: This cartoon jokes that neutrophils can 'shoot traps' to catch pathogens. What is the actual name of this antimicrobial process?

explanation.summary: Neutrophils extrude webs of decondensed chromatin (DNA) studded with antimicrobial proteins such as myeloperoxidase and elastase that trap and kill extracellular microbes. This process is called NETosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neutrophils extrude webs of decondensed chromatin (DNA) studded with antimicrobial proteins such as myeloperoxidase and elastase that trap and kill extracellular microbes. This process is called NETosis.

questions.stem: These cultured cells display long, thin cytoplasmic veils/processes and are the most potent activators of naive T cells. What cell type are they?

explanation.summary: Dendritic cells extend numerous membrane processes that increase surface area for antigen capture and presentation. They are the principal professional antigen-presenting cells that prime naive T lymphocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dendritic cells extend numerous membrane processes that increase surface area for antigen capture and presentation. They are the principal professional antigen-presenting cells that prime naive T lymphocytes.

questions.stem: The IL-12 / IFN-gamma feedback loop shown between a T cell and a macrophage is essential for eliminating which type of pathogen?

explanation.summary: Macrophage-derived IL-12 drives Th1 (and NK) cells to secrete IFN-gamma, which classically activates macrophages to kill phagocytosed intracellular organisms. Defects in this axis (e.g., IL-12 or IFN-gamma receptor mutations) cause susceptibility to mycobacteria.
explanation.whyCorrect: Macrophage-derived IL-12 drives Th1 (and NK) cells to secrete IFN-gamma, which classically activates macrophages to kill phagocytosed intracellular organisms. Defects in this axis (e.g., IL-12 or IFN-gamma receptor mutations) cause susceptibility to mycobacteria.

questions.stem: Identify the predominant white blood cells in this smear: cells with a multilobed (3-5 lobe) nucleus and pale, finely granular cytoplasm.

explanation.summary: Segmented neutrophils have a nucleus of 3-5 lobes joined by thin strands and neutral (pale) cytoplasmic granules. They are the most abundant circulating leukocyte and the first responders in acute bacterial infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Segmented neutrophils have a nucleus of 3-5 lobes joined by thin strands and neutral (pale) cytoplasmic granules. They are the most abundant circulating leukocyte and the first responders in acute bacterial infection.

questions.stem: In this peripheral blood smear, identify the largest leukocyte, which has abundant blue-gray cytoplasm and a folded, kidney-shaped (indented) nucleus.

explanation.summary: Monocytes are the largest circulating leukocytes, with a folded reniform nucleus and abundant gray-blue cytoplasm. They migrate into tissues to become macrophages. The smaller multilobed cells present are neutrophils.
explanation.whyCorrect: Monocytes are the largest circulating leukocytes, with a folded reniform nucleus and abundant gray-blue cytoplasm. They migrate into tissues to become macrophages. The smaller multilobed cells present are neutrophils.

questions.stem: In this blood smear, identify the granulocyte with a bilobed nucleus packed with coarse red-orange (eosinophilic) granules.

explanation.summary: Eosinophils have a bilobed nucleus and large red-orange granules. They defend against helminths and participate in allergic (type I hypersensitivity) reactions; their granules contain major basic protein.
explanation.whyCorrect: Eosinophils have a bilobed nucleus and large red-orange granules. They defend against helminths and participate in allergic (type I hypersensitivity) reactions; their granules contain major basic protein.
